lds.mormon_label:
The word Mormon comes from the Book of Mormon, the scripture that members of the church accept, and it has long been used as a nickname for members and for the church. Members have often used it themselves, and it has been widely accepted.

In 2018 the president of the church asked that the full name, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, be used, and that the nicknames Mormon Church and LDS Church be avoided, since the name emphasizes Jesus Christ. Members are called Latter-day Saints, and the word Mormon may still be used in terms such as Book of Mormon. A Protestant reader who has used Mormon to refer to the church should note that the church's own preference is now for its full name, or for Latter-day Saints, and that this is a matter of respect.
catholic.mortal_and_venial_sin:
Catholics distinguish between mortal and venial sin, drawing on the teaching in the First Letter of John that there is sin which leads to death and sin which does not. A mortal sin is a grave offense committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent. It destroys the love of God in the heart and cuts a person off from grace, and it must be confessed in the sacrament of Reconciliation before receiving communion.

A venial sin is a lesser offense, or a serious one committed without full knowledge or full consent. It wounds but does not destroy a person's relationship with God, and it can be forgiven through prayer, the Mass and acts of charity. Protestants generally teach that all sin deserves God's judgment and is forgiven in Christ, without the same classification. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics use the distinction to describe how sin affects the soul's friendship with God.
ortho.mortal_and_venial_sin:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not use the Western categories of mortal and venial sin. It understands sin as missing the mark, and as a sickness of the soul that damages a person's relationship with God, and it speaks of the passions, meaning disordered desires that enslave the person, and of the need to be healed of them.

Every sin harms, and every sin needs repentance, and the church's confession is offered as healing. Some serious sins, such as murder or apostasy, are treated more strictly, and may lead to a period of separation from communion and a penance. Yet the church avoids a legal scale. A Protestant reader who thinks of sin as breaking God's law, and as needing forgiveness, will find that the Orthodox agree that sin needs forgiveness, but see it more as an illness to be cured than as a crime to be punished.
jehovahs_witnesses.name_of_god:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that God has a personal name, Jehovah, the common English form of the four Hebrew letters known as the Tetragrammaton. They believe that the name appears thousands of times in the Hebrew Scriptures and that Jesus made it known to his followers. Their own Bible translation uses Jehovah where the original letters appear, and in some other places.

Using and honoring the divine name is central to their faith and identity. They take the name Jehovah's Witnesses from a passage in the book of Isaiah where God calls his people his witnesses. Many Protestant Bibles render the four letters as LORD in capital letters, following Jewish custom, and Protestants generally regard the use of the name Jehovah or Yahweh as permissible but not necessary. A Protestant reader should note that Witnesses treat using the name as a duty and a privilege.
lds.name_of_god:
Latter-day Saints teach that the names of God express who he is, and that different names refer to different members of the Godhead. They use the name Elohim for God the Father, and they teach that Jehovah, the name that appears as the LORD in many Old Testament passages, is the premortal Jesus Christ.

This differs from the more common Protestant understanding that the LORD of the Old Testament is the one God, the Father, the Son and the Spirit together, or is the Father. Latter-day Saints address their prayers to Heavenly Father, in the name of Jesus Christ. A Protestant reader will find that Latter-day Saints use the same names of God, but assign them differently, in accordance with their teaching that the Father and the Son are separate beings.
messianic.name_of_god:
In Messianic Judaism, God's name is written YHVH, the four letters given in the Hebrew Scriptures. Following Jewish custom, many Messianic believers avoid pronouncing the name casually and say Hashem, which means the Name, out of reverence. Practice differs, and some congregations pronounce a form of the name in worship.

Messianic believers also use the Hebrew name Yeshua for Jesus, since it is the name by which he would have been known among his own people, and it means salvation. Using it is a way of stressing his Jewish identity and the Jewish roots of the faith. Most Messianic believers affirm that Yeshua is the Messiah and is one with God, though language about this varies. A Protestant reader should note that Messianic believers keep Jewish customs of reverence for God's name alongside faith in Jesus.
oneness_pentecostal.name_of_god:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that Jesus is the name of the one God in his redemptive work: the name given to the Father's manifestation in the Son, and the name above every name. They point to New Testament passages where healings, miracles, prayer, baptism and teaching are done in the name of Jesus.

For them, to speak of the name of Jesus is to speak of God's own name for the age of salvation. It is used in worship, in prayer, in blessing and above all in baptism, where the name is spoken over the person being baptized. Members regard this as more than a formula, since to call on the name of Jesus is to call on God himself. A Protestant reader who holds that Jesus is the Son, distinct from the Father, should note that Oneness Pentecostals identify the name of Jesus with God himself.
catholic.natures_of_christ:
Catholics confess, with the Council of Chalcedon in 451, that Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division or separation. He is truly God and truly man, and the union of the two natures in the one person of the Son is called the hypostatic union.

The Church also teaches that Christ has two wills, a divine will and a human will, in harmony with each other, as decided at the Third Council of Constantinople. This teaching protects both the real humanity of Jesus, who suffered, was tempted and died, and his deity, which gives his acts saving power. A Protestant reader will find that Catholic teaching about the two natures is the same as the classical Protestant teaching, since Protestants generally accept the early councils.
church_of_the_east.natures_of_christ:
The Church of the East, which includes the Assyrian Church of the East, teaches that Christ has two natures, divine and human, each with its own property, united in one person, whom the church calls the one parsopa of the Son. It uses the Syriac word qnoma for the individual property of each nature, and speaks of two qnome, and is called dyophysite.

Other churches have sometimes called this church Nestorian, after Nestorius, a label the Assyrian Church rejects. In 1994 its patriarch and Pope John Paul II signed a Common Christological Declaration, stating that they share the same faith in Christ. A Protestant reader who confesses the two natures of Christ should note that this church holds the same doctrine, and that the disagreements that separated it from others are largely disagreements about words.
jehovahs_witnesses.natures_of_christ:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus is the Son of God, and that he is a created being: the firstborn of all creation, and the one through whom Jehovah made everything else. He is mighty and honored, and is called a god in a sense that shows his high position, but he is not equal to the Almighty Jehovah.

Witnesses hold that when he came to earth he became a perfect human, and that he gave his human life as a ransom sacrifice to buy back what was lost through Adam's sin. They regard him as the only one through whom salvation comes, and as the ruling King of God's Kingdom. A Protestant reader who confesses that Christ is fully God and fully man should note that Witnesses do not accept that he is God, and hold instead that he is a separate and lesser being.
lds.natures_of_christ:
Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ is both divine and mortal. From his mother Mary he inherited mortality, which made it possible for him to suffer and to die, and from his Father, God, he inherited divine power, including power over death. They teach that this combination made his Atonement possible.

They do not use the language of two natures united in one person, as in the creeds of Nicaea and Chalcedon, since they hold that Christ is a separate being from the Father, though united with him in purpose. A Protestant reader who confesses that Christ is fully God and fully man will find that Latter-day Saints also confess that he is divine, and truly human, but describe his identity and relationship to the Father differently.
oneness_pentecostal.natures_of_christ:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man: the one God manifested in the flesh, as the First Letter to Timothy puts it. In Jesus there is real deity, since he is the one God himself, and real humanity, with a human body, soul and will.

Many Oneness believers understand the title Son of God as referring especially to the humanity of Jesus, the flesh which the eternal God took on, while the deity dwelling in it is the Father. They generally do not speak of an eternal Son distinct from the Father. A Protestant reader who confesses two natures in one person of the eternal Son should note that Oneness Pentecostals affirm the full deity and humanity of Jesus, but explain it without the doctrine of the Trinity.
oriental_ortho.natures_of_christ:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, confess that Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word, following Cyril of Alexandria, an approach often called miaphysite. They teach that in Christ divinity and humanity are united in one nature, without confusion, mixture or change, and that he is fully God and fully man.

They reject the label monophysite, which suggests that Christ's humanity was absorbed into his divinity, and they condemn the teaching of Eutyches, who held that. They did not accept the Council of Chalcedon's language of two natures because they felt that it risked dividing Christ. A Protestant reader who confesses the Chalcedonian formula should note that these churches share the belief that Christ is fully God and fully man, and that the difference is largely one of terminology.
ortho.natures_of_christ:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses, with the Council of Chalcedon in 451, that Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division or separation. He is truly God and truly man, and the union takes place in the one person of the Son.

The Orthodox also affirm, with the Third Council of Constantinople, that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in harmony with each other. This protects both his real humanity, and his deity, which gives his acts saving power. The Orthodox also stress that Christ took on a whole human nature in order to heal it. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox teaching about the two natures is the same as classical Protestant teaching, as Protestants have generally accepted the early councils.
evangelical.new_birth:
Evangelicals use the phrase born again, drawn from Jesus' words to Nicodemus in the Gospel of John, to describe the new spiritual life that God gives when a person repents of sin and trusts in Christ. They call it the new birth, or regeneration, and understand it as the work of the Holy Spirit, which changes a person's heart and makes him a child of God.

Many Evangelicals are able to describe when it happened for them, and often speak of a conversion experience, though some cannot name a moment. It is usually distinguished from baptism, which Evangelicals generally understand as a public sign that follows. Protestants from other traditions understand the new birth differently: Lutherans often connect it with baptism, and Reformed Christians teach that God regenerates before a person believes. A Protestant reader should note that the phrase born again, for Evangelicals, points to a personal turning to Christ.
catholic.new_creation:
Catholics look forward to the new heavens and the new earth described in the book of Revelation. They teach that at the end of time the whole creation will be renewed and transformed, and that it will not be destroyed and replaced. The bodies of the saved will be raised and glorified, and the material world will share in the glory of God.

The Church holds that this new creation has already begun in Christ's resurrection, and that the sacraments and the life of the Church are foretastes of it. The hope includes the whole cosmos and not just individual souls. It is expressed in the Church's liturgy and prayer. A Protestant reader will find the language of new heavens and a new earth familiar from Scripture, and should note that Catholics stress the continuity between the present creation and the renewed one.
jehovahs_witnesses.new_creation:
Jehovah's Witnesses believe that God's purpose is for the earth to be a paradise, and that this purpose will be carried out under the rule of Christ. They read passages from the Psalms and from the book of Revelation as promising that the meek will inherit the earth, that death and sickness will be no more, and that people will live in peace forever.

They understand the new heavens to be the new government of God's Kingdom under Christ, and the new earth to be a new human society of obedient people on the renewed earth. The hope is for real life on a real earth, restored to what God intended in the garden of Eden. A Protestant reader who expects the redeemed to dwell in heaven should note that most Witnesses expect an earthly paradise, while a small group of anointed Christians expect to rule with Christ in heaven.
lds.new_creation:
Latter-day Saints teach that the earth will be renewed and receive its paradisiacal glory at the time of the Second Coming, as their tenth Article of Faith states. They believe that it will be cleansed and sanctified, and that eventually it will become a celestial kingdom, the dwelling of those who are exalted.

They see the earth as having a divine purpose, as a home created for God's children, and they expect the earth itself to be resurrected and glorified. Many Protestants speak of new heavens and a new earth, following the books of Isaiah and Revelation. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the expectation of a renewed earth, and connect it with the teaching that the righteous will live in the presence of God and continue to progress.
ortho.new_creation:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that Christ's resurrection has begun a new creation, and that the whole creation, and not only human beings, is to be transfigured and made new at the end. The Orthodox understand salvation as involving the healing of the created world as well as of persons.

This new creation is already present in the life of the Church, in the sacraments and in the lives of the saints, who show what it is to be made new. Orthodox worship at Pascha, the Orthodox Easter, celebrates the resurrection as the beginning of the renewal of all things. It is often expressed through the use of matter, such as water, oil, bread and incense, as means of blessing. A Protestant reader should note that Orthodoxy tends to see the whole cosmos as included in God's redemption.
anabaptist.oaths:
Anabaptists do not swear oaths. They understand Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount, that his followers should not swear at all but let their yes be yes and their no be no, as a direct command. A Christian's word should be so reliable that no oath is needed.

In legal settings Anabaptists ask to make an affirmation in place of an oath, and many countries allow this. In some stricter groups, the objection also affects willingness to hold certain public offices or serve on juries where oaths are required. A Protestant reader from a church that permits oaths in court should note that Anabaptists see the conviction as being less about a formula than about truthfulness in every conversation, and about not suggesting that a person's ordinary speech needs any additional guarantee.
catholic.oaths:
The Catholic Church teaches that oaths are permissible when they are made truthfully, with justice and for a serious reason, since an oath calls God as witness to what is said. Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount is understood to forbid false, frivolous or unnecessary swearing, and not all oaths.

Catholics take oaths in court, in public office and in religious vows, and the Church recognizes that God himself is described in Scripture as swearing oaths. It warns against taking the name of God in vain, and against perjury as a grave sin. A Protestant reader from an Anabaptist or Quaker background, which rejects oaths altogether, should note that the Catholic teaching takes Jesus' words to concern the abuse of oaths and not their careful use.
quaker.oaths:
Friends do not take oaths. They understand Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount, and the teaching in the letter of James, to mean that a Christian's plain word should be enough: let your yes be yes and your no be no. To swear a special oath would suggest that a person is truthful only when under oath.

In courts and public life, Quakers ask to make a solemn affirmation instead, and many legal systems allow this. The testimony is really about truthfulness in all of life, not just refusal of a ceremony. A Protestant reader from a church that takes oaths in court should note that Friends aim to speak the truth at all times, so that no additional promise is needed to guarantee it, and that this is a matter of integrity rather than of ritual.
lds.offices_of_christ:
Latter-day Saints describe Jesus Christ through many titles and roles, rather than a fixed threefold scheme. He is the Creator, under the Father's direction, the Savior and Redeemer, the mediator and advocate with the Father, the judge of all, and the Messiah and King. They also identify him as Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament.

In the Book of Mormon and the Doctrine and Covenants he is also described as a prophet, a high priest and a king, so the traditional Protestant pattern is not foreign to them, though it is not organized as a doctrine of offices. A Protestant reader familiar with the Reformed idea of prophet, priest and king should note that Latter-day Saints speak of Christ's work through these and other roles, all centered on his atonement.
reformed.offices_of_christ:
Reformed teaching describes Christ's work through three offices, an idea often called the threefold office, or in Latin, munus triplex. As prophet, Christ reveals God's will and word. As priest, he offered himself once as a sacrifice for sin and continues to intercede for his people. As king, he rules over the church and the world and will finally defeat every enemy.

This pattern is used in Reformed catechisms and confessions, and is associated with John Calvin's teaching. It is meant to show the fullness of what Christ has done, and to describe the meaning of his name, Christ, which means anointed one: in the Old Testament, prophets, priests and kings were anointed. A Protestant reader from another tradition will find that many Protestants use the same threefold pattern, which has become widely shared, though it is particularly at home in Reformed teaching.
catholic.one_true_church:
The Catholic Church teaches that the Church which Christ founded, the one Church of Christ, subsists in the Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him. This is the language of the Second Vatican Council. It means that the Church of Christ is found fully and concretely in the Catholic Church.

At the same time the Council taught that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside its visible structure, and that other baptized Christians are joined to it in an imperfect communion. Salvation is possible for those who do not know the Catholic Church through no fault of their own. A Protestant reader who thinks of the true church as the invisible company of all believers should note that Catholics affirm a visible Church, and see other churches as sharing in it to varying degrees.
churches_of_christ.one_true_church:
Members of Churches of Christ speak of the church of Christ, using a biblical name, to mean the body of all who belong to Christ and follow the New Testament pattern. Many say that they wish to be Christians only, not a denomination, and they avoid denominational titles and creeds.

Historically, some in this tradition taught that only members of Churches of Christ were truly saved, and this view is still held by some. Many others today say that God alone knows who belongs to him, and that Christians exist in many fellowships. They continue to hold that the New Testament pattern for the church is worth following. A Protestant reader should note that most other Christians hear the name as a claim to exclusivity, and that members often address this directly.
iglesia_ni_cristo.one_true_church:
The Iglesia ni Cristo, which means Church of Christ, teaches that Christ founded one church and that this church is necessary for salvation. Members understand the New Testament to describe a single body that Christ purchased with his own blood, not a collection of equal denominations.

They teach that the church established by the apostles fell into apostasy after the apostolic age, and that God restored the true church in the last days. Because of this, members regard salvation as found within the Church of Christ. The emphasis is on unity of doctrine and on obedience to what members read as the plain teaching of Scripture. A Protestant reader who thinks of the true church as all believers in Christ should note that the Iglesia ni Cristo identifies the true church with their own organization.
lds.one_true_church:
Latter-day Saints describe The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as the only true and living church on the face of the earth, a phrase from their book of scripture, the Doctrine and Covenants. They mean that it is the only church which has the fullness of the gospel and the authority of the priesthood, restored through Joseph Smith.

They do not mean that no one else has truth or is close to God. Latter-day Saints teach that other churches contain much truth and do much good, and that people of all faiths are children of God. The phrase is about authority and ordinances, not about who is sincere or who is a good person. A Protestant reader should note that this is a claim about the organization and its authority, and that most other Christians find it exclusive.
ortho.one_true_church:
The Eastern Orthodox Church believes that it is the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church, the same Church that was founded by Christ and the apostles, and that it has kept the fullness of the faith and sacraments through history. It does not regard itself as one denomination among others.

Orthodox teaching is generally cautious about judging the status of others. A common saying is that the Orthodox know where the Church is, but do not presume to say where it is not, leaving the salvation of other Christians to God. There are differences of opinion among the Orthodox on how far to recognize the sacraments of other churches. A Protestant reader who thinks of the true church as invisible should note that the Orthodox identify the Church with a visible community of bishops, sacraments and councils.
catholic.open_canon:
The Catholic Church holds that the canon of Scripture is closed. It teaches that the Bible consists of seventy-three books, and that public revelation, the revelation given for the whole Church, was completed with Christ and the apostles. No new books can be added to Scripture.

The Church does teach that its understanding of the faith can develop, and that God can give private revelations to individuals, but these do not add to the deposit of faith. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics and Protestants agree that the canon is closed, and that the disagreement between them is about which books belong to it, since the Catholic Old Testament contains seven more books than the Protestant one.
community_of_christ.open_canon:
Community of Christ treats Scripture as the church's foundation and understands it as open to continuing witness. The Bible is the primary scripture. The Book of Mormon is accepted as an additional scripture and a witness to Jesus Christ, and the Doctrine and Covenants contains counsel received by the church over time.

The church holds that God continues to speak, and that new counsel is tested and accepted by the church in common, sometimes being added to the Doctrine and Covenants. An example is the counsel that led to the ordination of women. Members hold different views about how to understand the Book of Mormon, for example whether to read it as history. A Protestant reader who holds to a closed canon of sixty-six books should note that Community of Christ believes revelation has not ended.
lds.open_canon:
Latter-day Saints hold an open canon of scripture. Their standard works are the Bible, which in English they generally use in the King James Version, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. They regard the Book of Mormon as another testament of Jesus Christ.

They believe that God continues to reveal his will through prophets, and that the canon may therefore be added to. Statements by the church's leaders, when approved by the church, are treated as scripture in some sense. A Protestant reader who holds to a closed canon of sixty-six books should note that the phrase open canon refers to the belief that revelation and scripture can still be given, and that Latter-day Saints treat the Bible as scripture but not as the only scripture.
seventh_day_adventist.open_canon:
Seventh-day Adventists hold to the canon of Scripture as sixty-six books, and they teach that the Bible alone is the standard of doctrine and life. They do not add other books to it. At the same time they believe that the gift of prophecy continues in the church, and that it was manifested in the ministry of Ellen G. White.

They call her writings the Spirit of Prophecy, and treat them as a source of guidance, encouragement and correction, but not as a second Bible. The church's own statements say that her writings are not a substitute for Scripture and must be tested by it. A Protestant reader who holds to a closed canon should note that Adventists agree with them about the canon, but accept a continuing prophetic gift that is subordinate to it.
baptist.ordination:
In Baptist churches, ordination is the act by which a local church recognizes that a person has been called by God to ministry, and sets him or her apart with prayer and the laying on of hands. It is usually done by the congregation, often with the participation of pastors from neighboring churches who examine the candidate.

Baptists do not treat ordination as a sacrament or as conferring special grace or authority, and they do not have bishops who ordain. It is understood as the church's recognition of God's call and of a person's gifts and character. Because each church is autonomous, standards for ordination vary. A Protestant reader from a church with a denominational ordination process should note that among Baptists the local church is the ordaining body, and that a person is ordained to serve, not into a separate order.
catholic.ordination:
In the Catholic Church, ordination is the sacrament of Holy Orders, in which a bishop, by the laying on of hands and prayer, ordains a baptized man as a deacon, a priest or a bishop. It is understood to confer a lasting spiritual character, so that a man ordained remains a priest permanently.

The Church teaches that Christ instituted the priesthood, and that priests act in his person, especially in celebrating the Eucharist and forgiving sins in Reconciliation. Only men are ordained, following Christ's choice of the twelve apostles, and in the Latin Church priests are normally celibate. A Protestant reader whose church understands ordination as the recognition of a call, and ordains women as well as men, should note that Catholics regard ordination as a sacrament which gives a special grace and a particular ministry.
lds.ordination:
In the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, ordination means conferring a priesthood office, by the laying on of hands by someone who holds the authority. Worthy male members are ordained to the Aaronic Priesthood beginning at age twelve, and later to the Melchizedek Priesthood, so that most adult male members hold a priesthood office.

The church has no professional or paid clergy. Local leaders such as bishops serve for a time in addition to their regular work, and are set apart for their calling by the laying on of hands, which is called setting apart, and is distinct from ordination. Women serve in many callings but are not ordained to priesthood offices. A Protestant reader accustomed to ordination as a rite for a professional pastor should note that in this church it is widely held by lay members.
ortho.ordination:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, ordination is called cheirotonia, meaning the laying on of hands, and it is one of the Holy Mysteries. A bishop ordains a man as a deacon, a priest or a bishop, during the Divine Liturgy, in front of the congregation, who respond by calling out that the candidate is worthy.

The Orthodox understand that it is Christ who ordains, through the bishop, and that the ordained receives grace for his ministry. Only men are ordained, and priests and deacons may be married if they marry before ordination. Bishops are usually chosen from among celibate clergy. A Protestant reader whose church treats ordination as the recognition of a call should note that the Orthodox regard it as a sacramental act in which the gift of the Holy Spirit is given, and in which the congregation takes part.
baptist.ordination_of_women:
Baptists are divided on whether women may be ordained as pastors, and because each church is autonomous, there is no single Baptist position. Many Baptist groups, such as the American Baptist Churches, the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship and many Baptist bodies in Britain, ordain women and have women serving as senior pastors.

Others, such as the Southern Baptist Convention, hold that while men and women are both gifted for service, the office of pastor is limited to men, and its confession of faith says so. Both sides appeal to Scripture, and they differ in how they interpret passages about the roles of men and women in the church. A Protestant reader should note that there is no unified Baptist stance, and that a Baptist church's position depends on its denomination and its own congregation.
catholic.ordination_of_women:
The Catholic Church teaches that it has no authority to ordain women to the priesthood, and that this judgment is to be held definitively. Pope John Paul II stated it in 1994, and it is based on the fact that Jesus chose only men as his apostles, on the constant practice of the Church, and on the understanding that the priest acts in the person of Christ.

The Church says that this is not a judgment about the worth or gifts of women, and it points to the many roles women hold in the Church, as religious sisters, theologians, teachers, administrators and, in some places, lay leaders of parishes. The question of women as deacons has been studied, and it has not been settled. A Protestant reader from a church that ordains women should note that Catholics see the matter as one of what Christ established, and not of equality or ability.
lds.ordination_of_women:
In The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, women are not ordained to priesthood offices, which are held by men. Women hold a wide range of leadership roles, however: they lead the Relief Society, the Young Women and the Primary organizations, serve as missionaries, teach classes and speak in worship services.

Church leaders have taught that women who are set apart for their callings, or who serve in the temple, act with priesthood authority delegated to them, even though they do not hold priesthood offices. Some members and groups have called for women to be ordained, and the church has not changed its practice. A Protestant reader from a church that ordains women should note that Latter-day Saints understand the priesthood as authority given to men, while affirming that women have essential roles in the church.
methodist.ordination_of_women:
Most Methodist churches ordain women as pastors and elders, and many have women bishops. In the Methodist tradition the call to ministry is understood as coming from God through gifts, grace and fruit, and the church's role is to test and affirm the call, whoever receives it. John Wesley himself accepted women as preachers when he saw evidence of their gifts.

In the United Methodist tradition, women have been granted full clergy rights since the middle of the twentieth century. Some smaller and more conservative Wesleyan bodies differ, and members can hold varying personal views. A Protestant reader should note that Methodists see women's ordination as a natural outgrowth of the belief that God's grace is offered to all and that all may be called to serve, and that it is one of the practices which distinguishes them from Catholic and Orthodox churches.
ortho.ordination_of_women:
The Eastern Orthodox Church ordains only men to the priesthood and the episcopate. It bases this on Christ's choice of male apostles, on the continuous practice of the church since the apostles, and on an understanding of the priest as an icon of Christ. Orthodox teaching holds that the difference in roles does not imply a difference in worth, and honors women saints, including Mary, the mother of God.

In the early church there were deaconesses, women who served in specific ministries, especially at baptisms of women, and some Orthodox theologians and churches in recent years have discussed or renewed the order in some form. The question of its nature is debated. A Protestant reader from a church that ordains women should note that the Orthodox present the matter as one of faithfulness to what the church has received, and not of deciding who is more capable.
catholic.original_sin:
Catholics teach that original sin is the condition into which every human being is born, as a result of the first disobedience of Adam and Eve. It is a state of deprivation: human beings lack the holiness and friendship with God that Adam and Eve had, and are subject to suffering, death and an inclination to sin.

Catholic teaching does not describe original sin as a personal fault of the newborn child. It is a privation and a state, inherited and not committed. Baptism removes it and gives new life, though the inclination to sin remains as something to struggle with. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, which speaks of inherited guilt and total corruption, should note that Catholics stress the loss of grace and the wounding of human nature, while affirming that human beings are not utterly corrupt.
lds.original_sin:
Latter-day Saints do not teach original sin. Their second Article of Faith says that people will be punished for their own sins and not for Adam's transgression. They believe that children are born innocent, and that they become accountable for their own actions at about the age of eight.

They do teach the Fall: Adam and Eve's choice to eat the fruit brought mortality, physical death and separation from God's presence, which affects everyone. Yet they see this as a necessary step in God's plan, which made agency, growth and family possible, and Eve is honored for her role. A Protestant reader who holds that all people inherit guilt from Adam should note that Latter-day Saints view the Fall as a positive and necessary event, and the inheritance as mortality and the need for redemption, but not guilt.
oriental_ortho.original_sin:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, teach the doctrine of ancestral sin, often described as the fall. They hold that through the disobedience of Adam and Eve, human beings inherited death and corruption, and a tendency to sin, but they generally do not teach that people inherit the guilt of Adam's sin.

Baptism is understood as washing away sin and giving new life in Christ, and infants are baptized. Christ is the new Adam who heals the effects of the fall. These churches share this understanding with the Eastern Orthodox. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, which speaks of inherited guilt, should note that these churches stress mortality and the damage to human nature, and see salvation as healing and restoration.
ortho.original_sin:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of ancestral sin, and of the fall. It teaches that through Adam's disobedience, death and corruption entered the world, and that all human beings are born into a condition of mortality and a tendency to sin. It does not teach that people inherit Adam's guilt, and holds that each person is responsible for his own sins.

Baptism washes away sin and begins a new life, though the struggle against the passions continues. Christ, the new Adam, undoes the effects of the fall, and human nature is healed in him. A Protestant reader, especially in the Reformed tradition, should note that Orthodox teaching places the emphasis on death and illness rather than on legal guilt, and that this affects how the Orthodox understand salvation as healing and growth.
reformed.original_sin:
Reformed churches teach that Adam was the representative head of the human race, an idea called federal headship: in his disobedience all his descendants are counted guilty, and all inherit a corrupt nature. They draw on the Letter to the Romans, which sets Adam and Christ side by side as two heads of humanity.

Because of this, everyone is born guilty and with a nature inclined to evil, and cannot save themselves. Salvation is likewise understood in terms of Christ's headship: those united to him receive his righteousness as Adam's descendants receive his sin. A Protestant reader will find this familiar in the Reformation heritage, and should note that Reformed teaching includes both guilt and corruption, while some other Protestants stress only the inherited inclination to sin.
anabaptist.pacifism:
Anabaptists hold that Jesus' teaching to love enemies and not to return evil for evil applies to his followers in the world, and so they do not take part in war or in violence. Many use the word nonresistance, meaning that the Christian does not resist an evildoer by force but answers with love and patient suffering. Others prefer to speak of pacifism or peacemaking, and work actively for justice and reconciliation.

This conviction goes back to the early Anabaptists, some of whom suffered persecution because they refused to bear the sword. It has shaped a long tradition of conscientious objection and service work. A Protestant reader whose tradition follows the Reformers in accepting just war teaching should note that for Anabaptists peace is a mark of discipleship, and that they do not regard participation in war as compatible with following Christ.
catholic.pacifism:
The Catholic Church teaches the just war tradition: the use of armed force is permissible only under strict conditions, including a just cause such as defense against grave aggression, legitimate authority, a last resort after peaceful means have failed, a reasonable hope of success, proportionality in the means used, and a right intention. Civilians must not be targeted.

The Church also teaches that peace is a gift and a duty, that everyone should work to avoid war, and that those who choose the way of nonviolence, and conscientious objectors, deserve respect. Recent popes have spoken strongly against war and against the arms trade. A Protestant reader will find that the just war tradition is shared by many Protestant churches, since the Reformers inherited it, and should note that Catholics also honor pacifism as a personal vocation, though not as a requirement for all.
mennonite.pacifism:
Mennonites speak of a peace witness: the conviction that following Jesus means refusing to take part in violence and answering hostility with love, as taught in the Sermon on the Mount. It grows from the Anabaptist heritage of nonresistance, and it has shaped Mennonite history, including conscientious objection to military service and a strong tradition of relief and service work.

The peace witness is understood as part of discipleship and not only as a political opinion. It also reaches into daily life, such as how conflict is handled in families and congregations. Practice is not identical everywhere, and in some places individual Mennonites have chosen military service. A Protestant reader whose church accepts just war teaching should note that for Mennonites peace is central to being a Christian, and is the shared center of a whole family of churches.
quaker.pacifism:
Friends hold the peace testimony: the witness that Christ's way leaves no place for war or violence, and that Christians are called to live in a way that takes away the occasion for it. Friends have historically refused military service and worked instead for reconciliation, relief and justice.

It is called a testimony because it is understood as a way of living that bears witness to the kingdom of God, rather than as a rule imposed from outside. Many Friends apply it to daily conflicts as well as to war. Not all Quakers hold it in the same way. Some meetings treat it as central and binding, while others leave it to each member's conscience. A Protestant reader whose church accepts just war teaching should note that for Friends the testimony grows from the belief that there is that of God in everyone.
catholic.papacy:
Catholics believe that the pope, the Bishop of Rome, is the successor of the apostle Peter, and the visible head of the whole Church on earth. He is also called the Vicar of Christ and the Supreme Pontiff, and he calls himself the servant of the servants of God. Catholics hold that Christ gave Peter a special role, and that it continues in the office of the pope.

The pope has supreme authority to teach and govern the Church, and serves as the center of its unity. He is elected by the cardinals, and he is also head of the state of Vatican City. Catholics do not believe that he is without sin, or that everything he says is infallible. A Protestant reader who regards Christ as the only head of the Church should note that Catholics believe the pope serves as Christ's representative and as a sign of unity, and not as a replacement for him.
ortho.papacy:
The Eastern Orthodox Church regards the pope as the Bishop of Rome, and honors the historic place of Rome in the early church, when the Bishop of Rome was seen as the first among equals among the bishops. It does not accept that he holds universal authority over the whole Church, or that he is infallible.

The separation between East and West, which is usually dated to 1054, involved disagreements about the pope's claims and about doctrine, and the Orthodox have continued to reject the claims that developed in the medieval West. The Orthodox recognize the Patriarch of Constantinople as first among equals among their bishops, but not as a ruler. A Protestant reader should note that Orthodox objections to the papacy resemble in some ways those of Protestants, and are based on the tradition of the early councils rather than on Scripture alone.
catholic.papal_infallibility:
Catholics teach that the pope is infallible when he speaks ex cathedra, meaning from the chair of Peter. This was defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870: when the pope, in his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is preserved from error by the Holy Spirit.

The teaching is very limited. It does not mean that the pope cannot sin, or that everything he says is without error, and it has been used very rarely, for example in the definitions of the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption. The Church also holds that the whole Church and the bishops together are preserved from error in teaching. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics see papal infallibility as protecting the Church's teaching, and not as giving the pope personal perfection.
old_catholic.papal_infallibility:
The Old Catholic churches emerged from a group of Catholics who refused to accept the dogma of papal infallibility and universal papal jurisdiction, as defined by the First Vatican Council in 1870. They hold that infallibility belongs to the Church as a whole, expressed in its councils and in the faith of the whole body of believers, and not to the pope by himself.

They kept the sacraments, the bishops and much of the worship of the Catholic tradition, and joined together in the Union of Utrecht. They regard the Vatican dogmas of 1870 as unacceptable innovations. A Protestant reader should note that Old Catholics are Catholic in worship and structure, and that their objection to papal infallibility is based on the tradition of the early church rather than on the Bible alone.
ortho.papal_infallibility:
The Eastern Orthodox Church rejects the doctrine of papal infallibility. It holds that infallibility belongs to the whole Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, and that it is expressed in the teaching of the councils as received by the whole body of believers, not in the person of any one bishop.

The Orthodox regard the definition of the pope's infallibility in 1870 as a new teaching, without basis in the early church, and as one of the obstacles to reunion. They emphasize that no bishop is above the church's tradition, and that even a council must be accepted by the faithful to be authoritative. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox share the Protestant objection to papal infallibility, but hold that the Church itself is preserved in the truth, which Protestants often locate in Scripture alone.
catholic.papal_primacy:
Catholics teach that Jesus gave Peter a special place among the apostles, when he said that he would build his Church on him and give him the keys of the kingdom, as recorded in the Gospel of Matthew. They believe that this role continues in Peter's successors, the bishops of Rome, who hold a primacy over the whole Church.

This primacy is understood as a primacy of jurisdiction, meaning real authority to govern and to teach, and it is described as a ministry of unity, sometimes called the Petrine ministry. It is affirmed by the First and Second Vatican Councils. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics understand the pope's authority as a service to the unity of the Church, based on Scripture and the practice of the early Church, and that Protestants generally do not accept it.
old_catholic.papal_primacy:
The Old Catholic churches accept that the Bishop of Rome has a primacy of honor, as the first among equals among the bishops, and can serve as a center of unity, as in the early church. They do not accept the teaching of the First Vatican Council in 1870 that he holds universal jurisdiction over the whole Church.

They regard the papal claims defined in 1870 as departures from the tradition of the first millennium. Old Catholics have been involved in dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church and with other churches about the nature of primacy. A Protestant reader should note that Old Catholics keep a form of Roman primacy, but limited, as a ministry of honor and service, and that they have their own structure of bishops under the Archbishop of Utrecht.
oriental_ortho.papal_primacy:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, do not accept the pope's claim to universal jurisdiction over the whole Church. They regard the bishops as equal in ministry, and they govern themselves through their own patriarchs and synods. The head of the Coptic Orthodox Church is himself called the Pope of Alexandria.

They respect the Bishop of Rome as an important bishop of the early church, and they have taken part in dialogues with the Roman Catholic Church about the meaning of primacy and about the common faith. A Protestant reader should note that these churches, like the Eastern Orthodox, agree with Protestants in rejecting papal authority, but do so on the basis of the early church's structure of bishops in councils.
ortho.papal_primacy:
The Eastern Orthodox Church recognizes that in the early church the Bishop of Rome held a primacy of honor, as the first among equals, in a church of many bishops, and it accepts that this primacy has an historical basis. It rejects the claims made in the medieval and modern West that the pope has universal jurisdiction over the whole Church.

For the Orthodox, the pattern of the early church is one of bishops governing their own churches and coming together in councils. Discussions between Orthodox and Catholic theologians continue about how primacy functioned in the first thousand years, and what it might mean today. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox willingness to recognize a primacy of honor is a difference from most Protestant churches, which have no such role for Rome, and that the Orthodox place their emphasis on councils.
catholic.perpetual_virginity:
Catholics teach that Mary was a virgin before, during and after the birth of Jesus, and that she remained a virgin throughout her whole life. This is called her perpetual virginity, and Catholics hold that it belongs to the faith of the Church from early centuries.

The New Testament speaks of the brothers and sisters of Jesus, and Catholics understand these words as referring to close relatives, such as cousins, following the wide sense of the terms in the language of the time. Some of the early Protestant Reformers, such as Luther, Calvin and Zwingli, also honored Mary as ever-virgin. Many Protestants today take the brothers of Jesus to be children of Mary and Joseph. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics see her virginity as a sign of her total dedication to God.
lutheran.perpetual_virginity:
Lutheran teaching honors Mary as the mother of the Lord and, in the Smalcald Articles of the Lutheran Confessions, calls her the ever-virgin. Martin Luther himself held that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life, and this view was common among the early Lutheran teachers.

Modern Lutherans differ on the point. Some continue to hold the traditional view as part of their heritage. Others regard it as a pious opinion that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, and so leave it a matter of freedom. What all Lutherans confess is the virgin birth of Jesus and Mary's honored place in the story of salvation. A Protestant reader should note that this is one of the places where early Protestant teaching was closer to Catholic and Orthodox teaching than many Protestants today are.
ortho.perpetual_virginity:
The Eastern Orthodox Church honors Mary as ever-virgin, in Greek aeiparthenos, meaning that she was a virgin before, during and after the birth of Christ, and throughout her life. The title was used by the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553, and it has been part of the church's faith and worship ever since.

The Orthodox tradition understands the brothers of the Lord in the Gospels as children of Joseph from an earlier marriage, or as other close relatives. The Orthodox regard Mary's virginity as a sign that she was wholly set apart for God, as the one through whom the Son of God became man. A Protestant reader who takes the brothers of Jesus to be children of Mary and Joseph should note that the Orthodox hold the ever-virgin teaching as a tradition received from the earliest centuries.
reformed.perpetual_virginity:
Reformed Christians confess the virgin birth of Jesus, and honor Mary as the mother of the Lord. On the question of whether she remained a virgin all her life, the tradition has not been uniform. Some early Reformed teachers, such as Zwingli, held that she did, but this is not a confessional teaching.

Many Reformed Christians today read the passages that speak of the brothers of the Lord as referring to Jesus' younger siblings, the children of Mary and Joseph, since this is the most natural reading of the text. Others regard the question as open, since Scripture does not settle it clearly. Reformed churches do not pray to Mary, and they do not make the perpetual virginity a matter of doctrine. A Protestant reader should note that the phrase brothers of the Lord is the point at which the Reformed usually take up the question.
baptist.perseverance:
Many Baptists hold that a person who is truly saved cannot lose his salvation, a teaching often called eternal security, and popularly summarized as once saved, always saved. They base it on passages such as Jesus' promise that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand.

Baptists explain that those who appear to fall away and never return were never truly saved in the first place. Calvinistic Baptists tie this to the perseverance of the saints, and stress that true believers will continue in faith. Not all Baptists agree: Free Will Baptists, for example, teach that a believer can fall away. A Protestant reader from a Methodist or Wesleyan tradition should note that most Baptists are on the other side of this question, and hold that God's keeping power guarantees the believer's final salvation.
catholic.perseverance:
Catholics teach that final perseverance is itself a gift. They pray for it and do not claim they can secure it by a past decision alone. A justified person can lose sanctifying grace by mortal sin, and restoration is possible through repentance and the sacrament of Reconciliation.

This is why Catholic life includes examination of conscience, frequent confession, and prayer against presumption and against despair. The Church also rejects anxious fear that God is unwilling to save. Perseverance is hoped for because God is faithful, and it is worked out because freedom remains real until death. A Protestant reader from a tradition that holds to eternal security should note that Catholics do not teach that a believer can be sure of finally being saved, and that they see salvation as a hope that must be kept alive.
evangelical.perseverance:
Many Evangelicals teach that a person who has truly been saved cannot lose that salvation, a doctrine known as eternal security, and often summed up as once saved always saved. They rely on passages that promise that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ, and that God will complete the work he has begun.

There are different versions of the doctrine. Those in the Reformed tradition teach the perseverance of the saints: true believers will endure in faith. Others emphasize that the believer's security does not depend on his performance. Evangelicals in the Wesleyan tradition teach that a believer can fall away from grace through persistent unbelief or sin. A Protestant reader should note that Evangelicals are not unanimous, though the belief in eternal security is widely held in many Baptist and independent churches.
lds.perseverance:
Latter-day Saints teach that salvation requires enduring to the end, a phrase from the Book of Mormon and from the Gospel of Matthew. They mean that a person must continue in faith in Christ, in repentance and in keeping covenants, throughout life. They do not teach that once a person has accepted Christ he is assured of exaltation.

It is possible to fall away, in their view, but a person who does so can always repent and return through Christ's atonement. Enduring to the end is not understood as earning salvation, but as remaining in the covenant relationship with God, sustained by his grace. A Protestant reader who holds to eternal security should note that Latter-day Saints stand with those who teach that believers must persevere, closer to the Wesleyan view than the Reformed one.
methodist.perseverance:
Methodists teach that a Christian can fall from grace. Salvation is a real relationship with God, and a person who has received it can turn away through persistent unbelief or willful sin and lose it. This is why Scripture contains warnings addressed to believers, and why Methodists take them seriously.

They do not teach that the fall is easy or the norm. They stress that God is faithful, that believers can have a real assurance of his love, and that the Holy Spirit keeps those who trust in Christ. A person who has fallen away may return through repentance, since God's mercy remains open. A Protestant reader who holds to eternal security should note that Methodists differ, and see human freedom as real to the end of life, though not as something to be anxious about.
reformed.perseverance:
Reformed churches teach the perseverance of the saints: that those whom God has truly called and saved will continue in faith to the end and will not finally be lost. This is because God keeps them by his power, and the Holy Spirit who has begun the work will finish it.

It is not that believers never struggle or fall into serious sin. They may stumble, and Scripture warns them to take care, but the tradition holds that God will restore them. Those who finally fall away are taken to be people who never truly belonged to Christ, though they appeared to. The doctrine is sometimes summarized as preservation by God. A Protestant reader will find that this is close to the popular teaching of eternal security, though Reformed teachers stress that true faith perseveres and does not merely have a past moment.
anglican.polity:
Anglican churches are governed by an episcopal polity: bishops have oversight of dioceses, and the church is led by bishops together with clergy and laity. Most Anglican provinces have synods with houses of bishops, clergy and laity, where decisions about doctrine, worship and order are made together.

Each national or regional church is self-governing, and together they form the Anglican Communion, a fellowship of churches which are in communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury. He is a focus of unity and is honored as first among equals, but he does not rule the other provinces. A Protestant reader from a church with no bishops should note that Anglicans keep the office of bishop but govern with synods, and that the Communion is held together more by shared heritage and prayer than by a single authority.
baptist.polity:
Baptists practice congregational government: each local church governs itself, under the headship of Christ, by the vote of its members. The congregation calls its pastor, receives and disciplines members, elects its leaders and manages its own affairs, without any bishop or higher body having authority over it.

Baptist churches join voluntarily in associations and conventions for mission, education and fellowship, but these serve the churches and do not rule them. The conviction is that Christ is present among the gathered believers and that every member has a voice in discerning his will. A Protestant reader from a church governed by bishops or by a presbytery should note that in Baptist polity the local congregation is the final earthly authority, and that this is understood as reflecting the New Testament pattern.
catholic.polity:
The Catholic Church is governed by a hierarchy: the pope, the bishops in communion with him, and under the bishops, priests and deacons. The world is divided into dioceses, each led by a bishop, and dioceses are divided into parishes led by priests. The pope and the bishops together are responsible for the whole Church.

The Church has its own body of law, called canon law, and it has regional and international bodies of bishops, and the Roman Curia which helps the pope govern. Lay people take part in councils and offices, and they have a voice, but authority to teach and govern belongs to the ordained. A Protestant reader from a congregational or presbyterian church should note that the Catholic Church is governed from the top, as an episcopal system with a universal head, and that this is regarded as part of what Christ established.
congregational.polity:
Congregationalists hold to congregational polity: the local congregation is a complete church under Christ and governs itself. The members together call their pastor, receive and dismiss members, and oversee their own property and ministry, rather than receiving these decisions from a bishop or a higher court. The bond among members is often expressed as a covenant made before God and one another.

Congregational churches do join together in associations and conferences for fellowship, shared mission and mutual counsel. These bodies advise and support, but they are not understood to rule the local church. A Protestant reader from a Presbyterian or Anglican church should note that Congregationalists give final authority to the assembled members, and that how much weight regional bodies carry differs from one Congregationalist group to another.
ortho.polity:
The Eastern Orthodox Church is governed by bishops acting together, an approach called conciliarity or synodality, in which decisions are made in councils and synods. There is no single head of the whole church on earth. Each bishop leads his own diocese, and the bishops of a region meet in a synod.

The Orthodox Church is made up of self-governing churches, such as those of Constantinople, Moscow, Greece, Romania, Antioch and others, which are in communion with each other. The Patriarch of Constantinople is honored as first among equals, but does not rule the others. Laity and clergy also take part in the life of the church, and in some churches in councils. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox have bishops, like Catholics and Anglicans, but govern through councils and not through a central authority like the pope.
presbyterian.polity:
Presbyterian polity means government by elders, called presbyters, who are chosen by the congregation. A local church is led by a body of elders, often called a session, and the churches of a region are joined in a presbytery, with larger bodies above it such as a synod and a general assembly. Authority rests in these councils working together, not in a single bishop and not in each congregation acting alone.

Decisions made at a higher level bind the churches below it, which is why Presbyterians describe their system as connectional. They hold that this pattern reflects the New Testament's picture of shared leadership and keeps any one person from holding unchecked power. A Protestant reader from a Baptist or Congregational church should note that in Presbyterian polity the congregation elects its elders, but the presbytery and higher courts have real authority over the local church.
catholic.prayer:
Catholics pray both together, in the liturgy, and alone. The liturgy includes the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, the daily prayer of the Church, and it uses set texts, including the Psalms. Personal prayer includes both memorized prayers, such as the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the Rosary, and quiet, unstructured prayer or meditation on Scripture.

The Church names several forms of prayer: blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving and praise. Catholics also pray to Mary and the saints, and ask their prayers, and they may use devotions such as novenas, a series of prayers over nine days. A Protestant reader who values spontaneous prayer should note that Catholics use spontaneous prayer as well, but place great value on the prayers of the Church, which they see as shaping how believers pray.
lds.prayer:
Latter-day Saints pray to God the Father, in the name of Jesus Christ, and end each prayer with the words in the name of Jesus Christ, amen. In prayer they use the older forms of address, thee, thou, thy and thine, as a sign of reverence. They usually bow their heads and fold their arms, and often kneel, in personal and family prayers.

Members are encouraged to pray morning and night, before meals, and as a family. Prayers are generally not read from a book, apart from the prayers used in the ordinances of the sacrament and others. Latter-day Saints also teach that prayer is a way of receiving personal revelation, and cite the invitation in the Book of Mormon to ask God whether its message is true. A Protestant reader will find that spontaneous prayer to the Father in Jesus' name is familiar.
ortho.prayer:
Eastern Orthodox Christians pray both in the church's worship and in private. Many follow a daily rule of prayer using the prayer book, with morning and evening prayers, including prayers to the Trinity, the Mother of God and the saints, and often pray in front of an icon corner at home. They make the sign of the cross and bow or prostrate as they pray.

The Orthodox also value the Jesus Prayer, and a tradition of inner prayer, called noetic prayer, meaning prayer of the mind and heart, associated with monks and hesychasts, in which the person seeks stillness and union with God. Spontaneous prayer also has a place. A Protestant reader accustomed to prayer in one's own words should note that the Orthodox tend to pray with the words of the church, and consider that they train the heart to pray.
catholic.prayers_for_the_dead:
Catholics pray for the dead, especially for the souls in purgatory, who are believed to be undergoing purification before entering heaven. They offer Masses for the dead, say the Rosary and other prayers, and give alms on their behalf. The Church sets aside November 2 as All Souls' Day, a day of prayer for all the faithful departed.

The practice rests on the belief in the communion of saints, which unites the living and the dead in Christ, and on the tradition of the Church from early times. Catholics also cite the passage in the second book of Maccabees which speaks of prayers for the dead. Most Protestants do not pray for the dead, since they do not accept purgatory and hold that a person's destiny is settled at death. A Protestant reader should note that Catholic prayer for the dead is an expression of love, and depends on belief in purification after death.
lds.prayers_for_the_dead:
Latter-day Saints care for the dead through what they call work for the dead. In temples, members are baptized on behalf of deceased people, by proxy, and also receive other ordinances for them. They ground this in a reference to baptism for the dead in the First Letter to the Corinthians, and in their teaching that all people should have the opportunity to hear the gospel and to accept it.

They believe that the dead in the spirit world are free to accept or to reject what is done for them. Members research their family history so that they can perform the ordinances for their ancestors, and it is a major reason for the church's interest in genealogy. A Protestant reader accustomed to praying for the dead, or not doing so, should note that this practice is an act of proxy service and not a prayer, and is central to Latter-day Saint temple worship.
oriental_ortho.prayers_for_the_dead:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, pray for the departed as a regular part of their worship. The liturgy contains commemorations of the dead, and memorial services are held after a death, and on set days, such as the third, ninth and fortieth day, in many of these traditions, and on the anniversary.

The prayers ask for God's mercy and rest for the departed, and the churches understand that the living and the dead remain united in the one body of Christ. They do not teach purgatory as the Catholic Church does. A Protestant reader who does not pray for the dead should note that these churches regard such prayers as an ancient part of Christian practice, and an expression of love which death does not end.
ortho.prayers_for_the_dead:
The Eastern Orthodox Church prays for the departed, and considers it an ancient and necessary part of Christian life. In the Divine Liturgy the names of the living and the dead are commemorated, and memorial services, called panikhida, are held after a death, on the ninth and fortieth days and on anniversaries. Certain Saturdays in the year are devoted to prayers for all the departed.

The Orthodox do not teach purgatory, but they believe that the prayers of the living help the dead, and that God is merciful. They sing Eternal Memory at funerals. A Protestant reader who does not pray for the dead should note that the Orthodox see this as a natural expression of the unity of the church, in which the living and the dead remain members of one body, and as a matter of love and hope for God's mercy.
catholic.preaching:
In the Catholic Mass, preaching takes the form of the homily, which follows the Gospel reading and is given by a priest or deacon. It explains the readings from Scripture and applies them to daily life, and it is required on Sundays and holy days. It usually lasts ten to twenty minutes.

Catholics understand the Liturgy of the Word, in which Scripture is proclaimed, as a real presence of Christ speaking to his people, alongside the sacramental presence in the Eucharist. The homily serves that Word and leads to the Eucharist, which is the center of the Mass. A Protestant reader who thinks of the sermon as the high point of a service should note that in Catholic worship the sermon is shorter and is one part of a service that culminates in communion.
ortho.preaching:
In the Eastern Orthodox Divine Liturgy, the homily follows the reading of the Gospel and is given by the priest or bishop. It is usually brief, and explains the day's readings or the feast, and applies them to the life of the congregation. Orthodox worship as a whole is understood as teaching the faith, through its hymns, readings and icons.

The tradition honors great preachers, such as John Chrysostom, whose name means golden mouth, and their homilies are still read. The liturgy, and not the sermon, is the center of worship, and the sermon serves it. A Protestant reader for whom preaching is the central act of worship should note that Orthodox worship gives it a modest place, and considers the sacraments and the prayers of the church as the primary way in which the faith is passed on.
reformed.preaching:
Reformed churches give preaching a central place in worship. They teach that when the Word of God is faithfully preached, God himself speaks to his people, and the sermon is a means by which the Holy Spirit creates and strengthens faith. The Second Helvetic Confession expresses this by saying that the preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.

For this reason the pulpit is usually the focus of the sanctuary, and Reformed pastors are trained to explain and apply the text of Scripture, often preaching through whole books of the Bible in order. The sermon is normally long and doctrinal, and is meant to teach as well as to move. A Protestant reader will find that the Reformed emphasis on preaching is widely shared in Protestant churches, though Reformed churches treat the faithful preaching of the Word as one of the marks of a true church.
catholic.predestination:
Catholics teach that God has predestined the elect to glory, and that this is a mystery of his grace. The Church holds that God desires the salvation of all, that he does not predestine anyone to evil, and that those who are saved are saved by his gracious initiative, while those who are lost are lost by their own free refusal.

Within that frame, Catholic theologians have differed on how grace and freedom fit together, from more Augustinian accounts to views that stress the real possibility of refusal, and the Church has not defined one school as the only Catholic one. It rejects the teaching that God is the author of sin, and that human freedom is a fiction. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition should note that Catholics do not teach an unconditional decree that determines who is saved and who is lost.
methodist.predestination:
Methodists teach that God's grace goes before us, and call this prevenient grace: God is at work in every person before they respond, awakening conscience and enabling them to hear the gospel and to answer freely. God desires all people to be saved, and Christ died for all.

For this reason Methodists do not hold to unconditional election, the teaching that God chooses some individuals for salvation and passes over the rest. They speak instead of a conditional election, in which God's foreknowledge sees who will respond in faith, and grace makes the response possible without forcing it. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition should note that Methodists distinguish their view from Reformed teaching, and that they say that human responsibility and God's grace both matter.
ortho.predestination:
The Eastern Orthodox Church speaks of foreknowledge more than of predestination. It teaches that God foresees everything, including how every person will respond, but that his foreknowledge does not cause anyone's choice or condemn anyone. God's will is that all be saved, and that no one is predestined to damnation.

When the Orthodox read passages such as those in the Letter to the Romans about those whom God foreknew and predestined, they understand them as describing God's plan to bring people to glory, and his knowledge of who would respond. Human beings are free, and salvation is a cooperation of God's grace and the human will. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, which teaches that God unconditionally chooses some for salvation, should note that Orthodox teaching rejects that view, and emphasizes God's love for all and human freedom.
reformed.predestination:
Reformed Christians teach predestination: that before the foundation of the world God freely chose those whom he would save, and that this choice is unconditional, based on his mercy and not on any foreseen faith or merit in the person chosen. Faith itself is understood as a gift which flows from this choice.

This is understood as a source of comfort and humility, and not as a cause for anxiety. It means that salvation is secure, since it rests on God's purpose. Reformed Christians differ on how to speak of those not chosen. Some speak of God passing over them, and others of a corresponding decree. They generally insist that human beings are still responsible for their choices, and that the gospel should be preached to all. A Protestant reader from the Methodist or Arminian tradition should note that Reformed churches reject the view that election depends on foreseen faith.
catholic.preexistence_of_christ:
Catholics confess that the Son of God existed before his birth as a man, and that he exists eternally with the Father. The Nicene Creed says that he is eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, light from light, begotten and not made. In the Gospel of John, the Word who was with God in the beginning is the one who became flesh.

It is the eternal Word, the second person of the Trinity, who preexisted, and not Jesus' human nature, which began at his conception. The Church teaches that the Son is equal to the Father, and that the Father and the Son are of one being. A Protestant reader will find that this is the same as the classical Protestant teaching that Christ is the eternal Son, a doctrine held in common by Catholics and most Protestants.
christadelphian.preexistence_of_christ:
Christadelphians teach that Jesus did not exist as a person before his birth. He existed beforehand in the plan and purpose of God, and the promises of a coming Messiah point toward him, but he came into being when he was conceived and born of Mary.

This matters to them because they hold that Jesus shared our human nature completely, and was tempted as we are, yet never sinned. Because of that, they say, he can truly stand in our place and be our representative before God. They read passages that speak of Christ before all things as describing what was in God's purpose. A Protestant reader who confesses that Christ is the eternal Son should note that Christadelphians hold that he was the Son of God only from his birth, and that they do not accept the Trinity.
jehovahs_witnesses.preexistence_of_chris:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus existed in heaven before he came to earth, as the first of Jehovah's creations and as his Word, the one through whom God brought other things into being. He is the only being created directly by God.

They also understand Jesus in his heavenly existence to be the archangel Michael, and they hold that Jesus is called by that name in his role as leader of the angels. This identification is based on their reading of passages in Daniel, Jude and Revelation. A Protestant reader who believes in the preexistence of Christ as the eternal Son, equal to the Father, should note that Witnesses hold that he was created, and had a beginning, and that he is not God in the same sense as the Father.
lds.preexistence_of_christ:
Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ existed before his mortal birth. They teach that he is the firstborn of the spirit children of Heavenly Father, and that in the premortal life he was chosen to be the Savior, and, under the Father's direction, created the earth. They identify him with Jehovah of the Old Testament.

In their view, all human beings also existed before birth as spirit children of God, so Jesus is the eldest among them, and yet unique in his divine role. Latter-day Saints do not teach that the Son is coequal and coeternal with the Father in the sense of the Nicene Creed, though they honor him as divine. A Protestant reader who says that Christ is the eternal Son should note that Latter-day Saints share the belief that he preexisted, and describe his relationship to the Father in terms of family rather than of a single being.
ortho.preexistence_of_christ:
The Eastern Orthodox Church confesses that the Son of God is eternally begotten of the Father, before all ages. This is often called eternal generation. It means that the Son has never been created and had no beginning, but has always been from the Father, as the Word who was with God in the beginning, in the Gospel of John.

The Nicene Creed says that he is begotten, not made, and of one being with the Father. In the Incarnation, the eternal Son took on a human nature, without ceasing to be God. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox teaching is the classical one that Protestants have generally inherited, though some Evangelical teachers question the language of eternal generation, and prefer to speak more simply of the eternal Son.
catholic.priesthood:
