Catholics speak of two forms of priesthood, both sharing in the one priesthood of Christ. The common priesthood belongs to all the baptized, who offer their lives, prayers and works as spiritual sacrifices. The ministerial priesthood belongs to those who have received the sacrament of Holy Orders.

The Second Vatican Council taught that the two differ in essence and not only in degree. The ordained priest acts in the person of Christ, especially in celebrating the Eucharist and forgiving sins, and serves the common priesthood of all the faithful. A Protestant reader who knows the phrase priesthood of all believers should note that Catholics affirm the common priesthood, but hold that it does not replace a separate ministerial priesthood, which Christ instituted for the service of the Church.
lds.priesthood:
In the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the priesthood is understood as the power and authority of God, given to men to act in his name in the church. There are two orders: the Aaronic Priesthood, the lesser, held by young men and including the offices of deacon, teacher and priest, and the Melchizedek Priesthood, the higher, which includes the offices of elder and high priest.

Priesthood is conferred by the laying on of hands, and it is held by almost all worthy adult male members. The church has no professional clergy, so the priesthood is used in a lay ministry, and its holders bless the sick, administer the sacrament and perform baptisms and other ordinances. A Protestant reader who thinks of a priest as a professional clergyman should note that in this church the word describes an authority held widely by lay men, and that a priest is also a particular office held by teenage boys.
ortho.priesthood:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, the priesthood consists of the ordained ministries of bishop, priest and deacon. Priests are ordained by a bishop and serve the church chiefly by celebrating the Divine Liturgy and the other sacraments, by teaching and by caring for the people. The bishop is the head of the local church, and priests act with his blessing.

The Orthodox also teach that all Christians are a royal priesthood, offering themselves and their prayers to God. The ordained priesthood is a particular ministry within the body of the church, and is understood as an icon of Christ, the great high priest, and not as a class apart. A Protestant reader who knows the priesthood of all believers should note that the Orthodox agree that all believers share in Christ's priesthood, but retain an ordained priesthood as part of the church's structure.
catholic.priesthood_authority:
Catholics teach that the authority of priests and bishops comes from Christ, and is given through the sacrament of Holy Orders. It is sometimes described as sacred power, and includes the power to teach in Christ's name, to celebrate the sacraments, and to govern the Church.

A bishop receives this authority in its fullness, and shares it with priests, who act as his co-workers. The priest's power to consecrate the Eucharist and to forgive sins in Reconciliation is understood as Christ's own action working through him. The authority is passed on through the laying on of hands, in the line of apostolic succession. A Protestant reader who thinks of ministerial authority as coming from the call of a congregation and the authority of Scripture should note that Catholics believe that it comes from Christ himself, through the unbroken succession of ordinations.
lds.priesthood_authority:
Latter-day Saints believe that God's authority to act in his name, the priesthood, was lost after the apostles, and restored through Joseph Smith by heavenly messengers: John the Baptist, who conferred the Aaronic Priesthood, and Peter, James and John, who conferred the Melchizedek Priesthood. Without this authority, they believe, ordinances such as baptism are not valid.

They also speak of priesthood keys, the authority to direct the use of the priesthood, which are held by presiding officers such as the president of the church, the stake presidents and the bishops. Those who hold offices exercise the authority within the limits of their keys. A Protestant reader who believes that a minister's authority comes from the call of the church and the Word of God should note that Latter-day Saints understand authority as a direct grant from God through an unbroken line of ordination.
